title: Making Muddy Water Clean
question: How can we make muddy water safe to drink?
steps: Clear is not the same as safe

steps.title: Water dissolves and carries things
steps.text: Water is very good at dissolving things. Salt and sugar dissolve in water and seem to vanish. Water can also carry things that do not dissolve, like tiny bits of soil. That is what makes muddy water look brown and cloudy.
steps.try: Press Add salt, then press Add mud.
steps.see: The salt disappears and the water stays clear. The mud makes the water brown and cloudy, with bits floating in it.

steps.title: Let it settle
steps.text: If you leave muddy water to stand still, the bits of soil slowly sink to the bottom. This is called settling. Big, heavy bits sink fast. Very tiny bits sink slowly, so the water can stay a little cloudy for a long time.
steps.see: A layer of mud builds up at the bottom of the jar, and the water above it becomes clearer.

steps.title: Build a water filter
steps.text: We can clean water even more with a filter made from a plastic bottle. Each layer has a job. Gravel at the top catches big bits like leaves and grit. Sand catches smaller bits of mud. Charcoal holds on to some of the things that cause bad smells, colours and tastes. Cotton at the bottom stops the sand and charcoal from falling out.
steps.try: Tap each layer's button to see its job.
steps.see: The water must pass through every layer, from the big gaps between the pebbles to the tiny gaps between the sand grains.

steps.title: Pour the muddy water
steps.text: Pour muddy water into the top of the filter. It trickles down slowly through the layers. Bits of dirt get stuck in the gaps, and much cleaner water drips out of the bottom.
steps.try: Press Pour muddy water. Press it again to pour more.
steps.see: Brown water goes in at the top. Much clearer water drips into the glass, and the top layers turn dirty brown.

steps.title: Clear is not the same as safe
steps.text: The filtered water looks clean, but it may still hold germs. Germs are tiny living things, far too small to see, and some of them can make us ill. A sand filter cannot catch them all.
steps.see: The magnifier shows germs swimming in the water that looked clean.

steps.title: Boil it before you drink
steps.text: Heat kills germs. Bring the water to a full boil, with big bubbles rising all the time, and keep it boiling for about one minute. Then let it cool and keep it in a clean, covered container. Always ask an adult to help with boiling water.
steps.see: The thermometer climbs to 100 °C, big bubbles rise and the germs die. Boiling does not take out salt or other dissolved things, though.

steps.title: Save water
steps.text: Clean water takes work to make, so we should not waste it. A tap that drips once every second drips 3,600 times in an hour and 86,400 times in a day. Over a year, that can add up to thousands of litres. Fix leaks, and turn the tap off while you brush your teeth.
steps.try: Turn on Fast forward. Then press Fix the tap.
steps.see: Drop by drop, the bucket fills up. Once the tap is fixed, no more water is wasted.

quiz.q: Which layer of a home-made filter catches the biggest bits, like leaves?
quiz.why: The water reaches the gravel first. Big bits get stuck in the gaps between the pebbles.

quiz.q: Filtered water looks clear. Is it safe to drink right away?
options: Yes, clear water is always safe
No, it may still have germs, so boil it first
quiz.why: A sand filter cannot catch all germs. Boiling the water for about a minute kills them.

quiz.q: What happens when muddy water stands still for a long time?
options: The mud slowly sinks to the bottom
quiz.why: Bits of soil are heavier than water, so they slowly settle to the bottom.
